note: Thin: 4 home, 2 foreign. No national chart existed; the year rests on one retrospective year-ranking (TurnTable), Tony Okoroji's industry memoir, a dated Omowura single and James Brown's late-1970 Nigerian tour. 'Happy Survival' is tied to the January 1970 end of the civil war, release year not confirmed. No juju, Hausa or gospel song could be tied to 1970.

Thin: 4 home, no foreign. 'Oroki Social Club' has a dated sales claim; Osadebe's single is dated 1971 by both his Wikipedia discography and TurnTable (the title was checked after a query and stands); 'Jeun Ko Ku' is documented as Fela's first Nigerian hit but the 1971 date comes from his discography. Rows whose source name ends '[dated release + general hit statement]' use the relaxed rule: release dated to this year (or the year before) plus a hit/popularity statement that does not name the year.

Moderate for Nigerian records, none for foreign ones. 'Fuel for Love' (TurnTable pick; one source dates it 1970), 'Board Members' (called Obey's all-time best seller) and 'Love Rock' (called the fastest-selling Nigerian single) are well attested. 'Help' is dated only 'c. 1972'. The last two rows are dated to 1972 but have weaker hit evidence (a group's 'first hits'; an all-time-greatest list). Rows whose source name ends '[dated release + general hit statement]' use the relaxed rule: release dated to this year (or the year before) plus a hit/popularity statement that does not name the year.

Moderate. Obey is the TurnTable pick; Ofege's debut is reported at 250,000 copies with both songs named as hits; 'Akula' is dated 1973 and described as scoring big. 'Give the Beggar a Chance' is called a massive hit but sources date it 1972 or 1973. 'Gentleman' is called a hit without a year in the source (1973 from discography). No foreign song could be tied to 1973. Rows whose source name ends '[dated release + general hit statement]' use the relaxed rule: release dated to this year (or the year before) plus a hit/popularity statement that does not name the year.

Thin to moderate: 6 home, 1 foreign. Sunny Adé's 'Esubiri Ebo Mi' (TurnTable pick) and 'Synchro System' (called his 1974 Nigerian hit) are the firm rows. 'Iheoma' is dated 1974 by Afrocritik, though another source ties its lyric to the 1975 Udoji award. Jimmy Cliff toured in December 1974 to a Beatles-scale reception, but no Nigerian source names which of his songs were the hits, so none is listed. 'Amanda' (1973 release) is placed a year after release on general evidence only. Rows whose source name ends '[dated release + general hit statement]' use the relaxed rule: release dated to this year (or the year before) plus a hit/popularity statement that does not name the year.

Obey's and Sunny Adé's 1976 Murtala tributes are dated but no source calls them hits, so they are left out. Moderate: 6 home, no foreign. 'Sweet Mother' (released December 1976, sales claims of 3 to 13 million) is the best-documented Nigerian hit of the decade. 'Fire in Soweto' is the TurnTable pick. 'Freedom' is called a runaway success for its label. 'Papa's Land' and 'Aka Bu Eze' are dated 1977 with only general hit statements. No foreign song could be tied to 1977 (FESTAC year).
